title: His Desire Is for Me
summary: The man praises the woman's beauty from her feet to her head in frank, lavish images drawn from jewels, harvest, towers, pools, and mountains, and he says he longs to climb the palm tree and take hold of its fruit. She answers that she belongs to her beloved and his desire is for her, and invites him out to the countryside and the vineyards, where she will give him her love.
story: Chapter 6 closed with a call for the Shulammite to turn back so that others could look at her. Chapter 7 is the longest and boldest description of her in the book. Earlier the man praised her from the head downward (4:1-7), and she praised him in the same order (5:10-16); here the gaze moves from her feet upward. The friction and searching of chapters 5 and 6 are now past, and the relationship is at its most confident. The woman's reply in verses 10 to 13 is the high point: she speaks of mutual belonging, then takes the initiative and invites him away. The book is nearing its close, and chapter 8 will move from delight to the book's great statement about the strength and cost of love.
historical:
The chapter's place names map the whole of Israel and its borders. Heshbon (verse 4) was a city east of the Jordan, once the capital of the Amorite king Sihon (Numbers 21:25-26), and excavations there have uncovered ancient water reservoirs, though linking a particular pool to this verse would go beyond the evidence. Bath-rabbim is otherwise unknown and may be the name of one of Heshbon's gates. The tower of Lebanon facing Damascus points north toward Aram, and Mount Carmel is the ridge that rises over the Mediterranean near modern Haifa. The purple of verse 5 was an expensive dye made from sea snails, associated with Phoenicia and with royalty.

The king in verse 5 is presumably Solomon, or the man playing the part of a king in the language of love, as bridegrooms in many cultures are honored as kings on their wedding day. As with the rest of the Song, the chapter cannot be tied to a specific year. Its sweep of geography, from Heshbon in the east to Carmel in the west and Lebanon in the north, fits a poet who knew the land well and wanted the beloved's beauty to fill it.
cultural:
Poems that praise a lover's body part by part are well known from the ancient Near East, and scholars often call them by the Arabic term wasf. Nineteenth-century travelers in Syria recorded village wedding songs in which the bride was praised in this way, and Egyptian love songs of the second millennium BC use similar imagery. The comparisons are not visual descriptions in the modern sense. A neck like an ivory tower suggests grace, pride, and value; eyes like pools suggest depth and calm; a nose like a tower of Lebanon suggests dignity rather than size. The images of wheat, wine, palm fruit, and clusters of the vine belong to a farming world where harvest meant life, abundance, and celebration.

The chapter speaks with a frankness that has made some readers uncomfortable, but its language is poetic and suggestive rather than crude, and the ancient readers who included it in Scripture evidently thought physical love within its right setting worthy of praise. The mandrakes of verse 13 were a plant with a strong fragrance and a forked root, which ancient people associated with love and fertility; in Genesis 30:14-16 Rachel and Leah bargain over them. The Hebrew word for mandrakes (duda'im) sounds like the word for love (dodim), a wordplay the poet surely intended.
literary: Verses 1 to 9 are the man's speech, organized as an ascending list from feet to head, then a summary exclamation (verse 6) and a new image of the woman as a palm tree (verses 7-9). The woman seems to interrupt in the middle of verse 9, taking his image of wine and turning it toward her beloved, and she speaks the rest of the chapter. Her words in verse 10 are the third and fullest form of a refrain of belonging (compare 2:16 and 6:3): this time she does not say he is hers but that his desire is for her. Verses 11 to 13 echo the spring invitation of 2:10-13, but now she is the one inviting. The recurring images of vines, buds, and pomegranates (compare 6:11) tie the woman to the fruitful land, and the garden, which in chapter 4 was an image of her, becomes a place they go to together.

outline.t: Praise from her feet to her head
The palm tree and its fruit
I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me
Come away to the fields and vineyards

doctrines.note: The chapter delights in the body and in the good things of the land (wheat, wine, fruit, fragrance) as gifts of the Creator. It gives no support to the idea that the body or desire is shameful in itself.

The mutual belonging of verse 10 describes love as it was meant to be between a husband and wife: freely given, delighted, and reciprocal. The woman is not an object of praise only; she speaks, invites, and gives her love.

Many readers hear in verse 10 a reversal of Genesis 3:16, where after the fall the woman's desire is for her husband and he rules over her. In the Song the man's desire is for her, and nothing is said of rule. Love here is a picture of what sin distorted, partly restored.

words.note: Teshuqah, desire or longing. It appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible: in Genesis 3:16 (the woman's desire for her husband after the fall), in Genesis 4:7 (sin's desire for Cain), and here. In Genesis the word belongs to a world bent by sin; in the Song it describes a man's glad longing for his beloved, which makes verse 10 one of the most striking echoes of Eden in the Old Testament.

Duda'im, mandrakes, a plant with a strong scent and a forked root that people in the ancient world linked with love and fertility. It appears only here and in Genesis 30:14-16. The word plays on dodim, love, the very thing the woman promises to give in verse 12.

Tamar, palm tree, the date palm, tall and slender, valued for its fruit. It is also a woman's name in the Old Testament. The image in verses 7 and 8 praises the woman's stature and grace and expresses the man's longing in a figure rather than in bare words.

christ: Like the rest of the Song, this chapter has no direct New Testament quotation, and its link to Christ is thematic. The church has long heard in the refrain of belonging an image of the bond between Christ and his people, and verse 10 especially has been read that way: the believer can say that she belongs to her Lord and that his desire is for her. The possible reversal of Genesis 3:16 also fits the larger story. The curse of Genesis 3 bent love between man and woman into rivalry and rule, and the gospel announces the undoing of the curse and the restoration of what God made good. Christians should be careful not to turn the body imagery of verses 1 to 9 into a code, as some older commentators did; the chapter's value as a window onto Christ lies not in hidden meanings but in its picture of faithful, joyful, self-giving love, which is what Christ's love is.

hard.q: Why does the Bible contain such frank physical imagery, and how should a reader handle it?
hard.a: Some readers are embarrassed by a chapter like this, and throughout history many preferred to read it only as allegory so as to avoid its plain sense. But the Bible does not treat physical love as dirty. Genesis presents man and woman as made for each other and naked without shame (Genesis 2:25), Proverbs urges a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth (Proverbs 5:18-19), and Paul tells married couples not to deprive each other (1 Corinthians 7:3-5). The Song gives voice to that goodness in poetry, and its language is veiled and figurative, not graphic. Most interpreters, including those who read it as describing a courtship, read it within the Bible's wider framework, where sexual love belongs to the covenant of marriage, and the book's own refrain warns against awakening love before its time (2:7; 3:5; 8:4). Readers who find the chapter uncomfortable are right to handle it with reverence, but reverence here means receiving the gift, not hiding from it.

questions: The man's praise is detailed and generous. What would it look like to notice and name what is good in the people you love?
In verse 10 the woman speaks with security rather than anxiety. What makes a person secure in love, and how does God's love for us relate to that?
Why might it matter that the Bible celebrates physical love instead of staying silent about it?
